paragraphs: A molecule’s three-dimensional geometry can be important for predicting its properties, but obtaining that geometry for every molecule is often impractical. This paper asks whether a graph neural network can learn useful geometric information during pretraining and later apply it when only a two-dimensional molecular graph is available.

The proposed method, 3D Infomax, uses existing datasets containing molecular geometry. It trains the graph network by maximizing mutual information between its representations and learned summaries of three-dimensional structure. The aim is to make the graph representation retain information connected to geometry. During subsequent fine-tuning, molecules do not need known three-dimensional structures for the network to use this implicit geometric information.

The authors report significant improvements across a range of molecular properties, including a 22% average reduction in mean absolute error on QM9 quantum mechanical properties. They also find that the representations transfer effectively between datasets occupying different molecular spaces. These findings support using available geometric data as a reusable training resource for property prediction.
icml-2022-3d-infomax-improves-gnns-for-m.tldr: 3D Infomax uses molecular geometry during pretraining to improve property prediction from two-dimensional molecular graphs.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses what to evaluate next using an acquisition function that expresses the value of a potential evaluation. Often, computing this function requires averaging a utility under a probabilistic surrogate model. Keeping that calculation manageable can restrict both the surrogate and the kinds of utility the optimization procedure can use.

Likelihood-free Bayesian optimization, or LFBO, directly models the acquisition function, removing the need for a separate probabilistic inference step with a surrogate. The authors show that acquisition computation can be formulated as a weighted classification problem. This generalizes an existing density-ratio estimation approach associated with probability of improvement and permits other utility choices within the same framework.

Using expected improvement as its utility, LFBO outperforms that earlier approach and several leading black-box optimization methods on the reported real-world problems. The method can also exploit composite structure in an objective, yielding further regret improvements of several orders of magnitude. The contribution connects a broader acquisition-function design space to a classification-based learning procedure.
icml-2022-a-general-recipe-for-likelihoo.tldr: LFBO learns acquisition functions through weighted classification, broadening Bayesian optimization beyond separately fitted probabilistic surrogates.

paragraphs: Biological sequence design presents a difficult setting for Bayesian optimization: candidate designs are discrete and high-dimensional, while many optimization techniques work most naturally with continuous variables. LaMBO addresses this mismatch by learning a latent representation in which it can optimize candidate designs using gradients.

The method jointly trains a denoising autoencoder and a discriminative, multi-task Gaussian process head. This combination supports gradient-based optimization of acquisition functions in the autoencoder’s latent space. Those functions guide the balance between exploring uncertain possibilities and exploiting promising ones over successive design rounds. They also support multiple objectives by seeking sequences at different points on the Pareto frontier, representing different objective tradeoffs.

The evaluation includes two small-molecule design tasks and newly introduced fluorescent-protein tasks involving computational and laboratory properties. LaMBO outperforms genetic optimizers in these experiments without requiring a large pretraining corpus. The results demonstrate a practical route for applying Bayesian optimization to the tested sequence-design problems while accommodating competing goals.
icml-2022-accelerating-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: LaMBO combines a denoising autoencoder with Gaussian process prediction to optimize biological sequences efficiently across multiple objectives.

paragraphs: This paper studies decentralized optimization when training samples are collected through a random walk and therefore depend on one another. The algorithm combines adaptive step sizes with momentum. The central theoretical question is how these choices affect convergence when the samples used for successive updates are dependent.

The authors establish convergence rates for both convex and nonconvex objectives. Their results show that adaptive random-walk algorithms can match the performance of a non-adaptive method for dependent data in general cases. They additionally prove acceleration when the stochastic gradients are sparse. Sparsity is therefore a stated condition for the stronger benefit, rather than a reason to expect acceleration in every problem.

The analysis also extends to a zeroth-order version of adaptive random-walk gradient descent, providing convergence results for that variant. The authors characterize their assumptions as mild and general, supporting applicability across many machine learning problems. Overall, the contribution gives theoretical support for adaptation under dependent sampling and identifies a particular gradient structure that can make it more advantageous.
icml-2022-adaptive-random-walk-gradient-.tldr: Adaptive random-walk gradient descent has convergence guarantees under dependent sampling and can accelerate optimization when stochastic gradients are sparse.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can choose small structures within network cells or larger arrangements of predefined blocks. The paper identifies different difficulties at these two scales: parameters used to select operations may not fully reflect their importance, while evaluating many sampled combinations of blocks can consume substantial time.

AGNAS uses attention to guide both kinds of search. An attention module follows each candidate operation in the micro search or each candidate block in the macro search. Its weights serve as indicators of the importance of those alternatives. This gives the two search settings a shared selection principle, linking architecture decisions to the attention assigned to candidate components.

The authors report 2.46% test error on CIFAR-10 using the DARTS search space and 23.4% test error when searching directly on ImageNet using the ProxylessNAS search space. They also report optimal performance on NAS-Bench-201, surpassing leading approaches there. These results support attention as a useful guide across the evaluated architecture-search settings and scales.
icml-2022-agnas-attention-guided-micro-a.tldr: AGNAS uses attention weights to guide the selection of operations and blocks in neural architecture search.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning reward surface describes how expected reward changes as a policy’s parameters change. Visualizing such surfaces can reveal why an optimization update succeeds or fails. This paper expands these visualizations to 27 widely used Gym environments, moving beyond the narrow settings previously explored.

The authors also inspect reward surfaces along the policy gradient direction. They find that many popular environments contain frequent cliffs: abrupt, large decreases in expected reward. In their demonstrations, A2C often crosses these cliffs into parameter regions with low reward, while PPO avoids them. This gives a concrete geometric explanation supporting a common intuition about PPO’s improved performance over earlier methods.

The paper contributes an extensible library so researchers can generate related visualizations themselves. Its findings make several agent failure modes visible in terms of the objective being optimized. The comparison provides evidence about update behavior in the studied environments, showing how the surrounding reward landscape can help explain differences between reinforcement learning methods.
icml-2022-cliff-diving-exploring-reward-.tldr: Reward-surface visualizations reveal abrupt reward cliffs that A2C often crosses and PPO avoids in the studied reinforcement learning environments.

paragraphs: An agent’s behavior can carry information while it performs a task. This paper formalizes communication of external information through trajectories in a Markov decision process as a Markov coding game. The setting captures a challenge in decentralized control when free communication is unavailable: conveying a message must be balanced against its effect on task performance.

The proposed method, MEME, combines maximum entropy reinforcement learning with minimum entropy coupling. This provides a theoretically grounded way to connect the communication problem with the agent’s decision process. Advances in approximation algorithms for minimum entropy coupling make the method usable in practical settings, extending its relevance beyond a purely theoretical construction.

Experiments show MEME outperforming a strong baseline on small games and performing well on extremely large ones. In particular, it communicates binary images without information loss through Cartpole and Pong trajectories while achieving maximal or nearly maximal expected returns. It also performs well with actuator noise. These demonstrations show that task behavior can support substantial communication alongside strong control performance.
icml-2022-communicating-via-markov-decis.tldr: MEME enables agents to communicate information through their task trajectories while maintaining strong expected returns in the demonstrated settings.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods can be studied through continuous-time models of their optimization trajectories. This paper develops an analysis based on changing coordinates before studying those dynamics. Instead of tracking the original position directly, it studies displacement from a reference point multiplied by a time-dependent scaling factor.

In these dilated coordinates, the authors derive a conserved quantity analogous to physical energy. That quantity provides a way to analyze acceleration and recover many existing continuous-time results through a streamlined approach. The method also yields new analyses of OGM-G, whose mechanism for rapidly reducing gradient magnitude differs from Nesterov’s acceleration mechanism.

The paper then connects this continuous-time viewpoint to a discrete optimization procedure. Applying a semi-second-order symplectic Euler discretization in the transformed coordinates gives an O(1/k²) convergence rate for the standard smooth convex minimization setting. The result does not require additional assumptions such as infinite differentiability. The coordinate transformation thus supports both clearer analysis of acceleration and a discretization with a stated optimization guarantee.
icml-2022-continuous-time-analysis-of-ac.tldr: Time-scaled coordinates reveal conservation laws for accelerated optimization and yield a discretization with an O(1/k²) rate for smooth convex minimization.

paragraphs: Random transformation defenses introduce stochastic processing into a neural network’s prediction pipeline, making their resistance to adversarial inputs harder to evaluate. An attack designed for a deterministic model may fail to expose their weaknesses. The authors show that the BPDA attack used to evaluate BaRT is ineffective and likely makes that defense appear more robust than it is.

The study strengthens both sides of the evaluation. The researchers select transformations and tune their parameters with Bayesian optimization to construct a strong defense, then develop an attack tailored to evaluating it. Their attack reduces accuracy by 83%, compared with a 19% reduction from the commonly used EoT attack, a reported 4.3-fold improvement.

These results indicate that the evaluated random transformation defense is not robust to adversarial examples on Imagenette. The authors subsequently use their attack for adversarial training, producing AdvRT and a large robustness gain. The study shows how stronger evaluation can both uncover weaknesses and supply training examples that help improve the defense.
icml-2022-demystifying-the-adversarial-r.tldr: A stronger attack exposes weaknesses in random transformation defenses and improves their robustness when used for adversarial training.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, an agent faces uncertainty from both its teammates’ actions and the environment’s transitions and rewards. These sources have different characteristics: teammates can adapt their behavior cooperatively, whereas the environment does not adapt in that way. Treating both sources through a single risk preference can obscure this distinction.

DRIMA introduces a framework for accessing and controlling sensitivity to the two sources separately. For example, an agent can take an optimistic view of teammates while remaining more risk-neutral about environmental randomness. This separation gives learning a way to express expectations about cooperation without requiring the same attitude toward unpredictable transitions or rewards.

Experiments on multiple StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge scenarios show significant improvements over prior leading methods. DRIMA also maintains robust performance in tested settings where earlier methods learn highly suboptimal policies, across reward shaping, exploration scheduling, and random or adversarial agent noise. The findings support separating sources of risk as a useful design choice for cooperative learning in these scenarios.
icml-2022-disentangling-sources-of-risk-.tldr: DRIMA separately controls sensitivity to teammate and environmental uncertainty, improving cooperative learning in the tested StarCraft scenarios.

paragraphs: Entropy regularization can help reinforcement learning, but it changes the objective and can shift the converged policy away from the original problem’s optimum. Divergence regularization offers a way to address this issue, yet transferring it to cooperative multi-agent learning requires additional work. This paper develops DMAC for that setting.

DMAC is an off-policy multi-agent actor-critic framework. The authors derive an update rule with theoretical guarantees of monotonic policy improvement and convergence in both the original and divergence-regularized decision processes. They state that the rule avoids regularization bias and also provide a bound on the discrepancy between the converged policy and the original optimal policy. This bound preserves a distinction between convergence and exact optimality.

The framework can be combined with many existing multi-agent learning algorithms. Evaluations in a didactic stochastic game and the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge show substantial performance improvements for existing methods. The contribution joins a theoretically analyzed regularization approach with a flexible framework for improving cooperative learning algorithms.
icml-2022-divergence-regularized-multi-a.tldr: DMAC brings divergence regularization to off-policy cooperative multi-agent learning, with analyzed convergence properties and empirical performance gains.

paragraphs: Differentiable simulators provide derivatives that could make reinforcement learning more efficient than relying on zeroth-order gradient estimates. Whether these derivatives produce better estimates is less clear in physical control problems involving complex landscapes and long planning horizons. This paper investigates factors that can undermine the expected benefit.

The authors show that physical characteristics such as stiffness and discontinuities may compromise first-order gradient estimation. They analyze these effects through bias and variance, examining the quality of the resulting estimate rather than assuming that access to derivatives makes it preferable. The stated difficulty concerns certain physical systems, so it does not imply that first-order methods are always ineffective.

The proposed alternative is an α-order gradient estimator, with α between zero and one, that combines exact-gradient information with zeroth-order estimation. It aims to bring together first-order efficiency and zeroth-order robustness. Numerical examples illustrate weaknesses of traditional estimators and advantages of this combined approach. The findings make simulator differentiation a question of estimator suitability as well as derivative availability.
icml-2022-do-differentiable-simulators-g.tldr: Differentiable simulators can yield problematic policy-gradient estimates, motivating an estimator that combines first-order information with zeroth-order robustness.

paragraphs: Predicting where and how a drug-like molecule binds to a protein is a central computational problem in drug discovery. Existing approaches can be expensive because they sample many candidates and then score, rank, and refine them. EquiBind instead predicts the binding location and the molecule’s bound pose and orientation directly.

The model uses SE(3)-equivariant geometric deep learning, connecting its predictions to the spatial structure of the problem. Its direct prediction covers blind docking, where the receptor binding location must also be determined. The authors report substantial speed gains and better quality than traditional and recent baselines. Combining EquiBind with existing refinement techniques improves results further while increasing runtime.

The paper also proposes a fast refinement method for the angles of rotatable ligand bonds. It uses closed-form global minima of a von Mises angular-distance objective relative to an input atomic point cloud. This replaces expensive differential-evolution strategies in that refinement step, adding a geometric adjustment mechanism alongside the direct docking model.
icml-2022-equibind-geometric-deep-learni.tldr: EquiBind directly predicts protein binding locations and ligand poses, achieving reported speed and quality gains with optional geometric refinement.

paragraphs: Some geometric learning problems use spaces such as hyperbolic space or the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices. This paper develops a fully connected neural network framework on noncompact symmetric spaces. Its construction includes hyperbolic neural networks and SPDNet as special cases, placing them within a shared mathematical treatment.

The framework builds on the Helgason-Fourier transform and introduces an associated ridgelet transform. For a continuous network with depth two, this transform maps a given function to network weights. It therefore supplies an analysis tool connecting functions on the geometric space to their representation by neurons. A coordinate-free formulation further identifies the role of nonlinear activations with that of a wavelet function.

The authors use a reconstruction formula to give a constructive proof of universality for finite networks on symmetric spaces. The significance is both architectural and theoretical: the work defines networks in this setting and connects their representation power to explicit transform machinery. The stated contribution centers on mathematical construction and approximation capability.
icml-2022-fully-connected-network-on-non.tldr: A Helgason-Fourier-based framework defines neural networks on symmetric spaces and gives a constructive universality proof through ridgelet reconstruction.

paragraphs: Mixup creates additional training examples by blending pairs of inputs. Although it generally improves prediction, it can sometimes reduce performance. This paper examines that failure through theoretical and empirical analysis, then develops a method intended to correct the labels assigned to the mixed examples.

The method, GenLabel, learns class-conditional data distributions using generative models. These distributions describe the data associated with each class and provide information for labeling mixup samples. The intervention therefore focuses on the supervision attached to an augmented example: generating a blended input and assigning it an appropriate class target are connected parts of the training procedure.

The authors use both theory and experiments to show that combining GenLabel with mixup can address the identified degradation and improve the accuracy of a mixup-trained model. The result supports using learned class distributions to improve augmentation labels. It is a qualified improvement claim: the paper shows that relabeling can resolve the problem, rather than establishing that every use of mixup or generative relabeling must improve performance.
icml-2022-genlabel-mixup-relabeling-usin.tldr: GenLabel uses generative models of class distributions to relabel mixup examples and can remedy mixup-related accuracy degradation.

paragraphs: Image inversion seeks a representation in a pretrained generator’s latent space that reconstructs a given image. This can make the generator’s learned image structure useful for restoration tasks. However, existing inversion methods produce suboptimal results when the input differs from the data on which the generator was trained.

SPHInX addresses this problem for StyleGAN-v2 by optimizing a style projection head with a training strategy that imposes vicinal regularization in latent space. This is the central mechanism for embedding out-of-distribution images more accurately. The approach can additionally optimize a content projection head and the noise variables in every layer to further enhance inversion.

On a suite of out-of-distribution data, the authors report higher-quality reconstructions than leading inversion techniques. They also find that SPHInX is effective for ill-posed restoration tasks and retains semantic editing capabilities. Together, these findings support adapting the inversion process so that a pretrained generator can serve a broader set of images while remaining useful for restoration and editing.
icml-2022-improved-stylegan-v2-based-inv.tldr: SPHInX improves StyleGAN-v2 inversion of out-of-distribution images through projection heads and latent-space regularization.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning needs substantial experience, so the speed at which training data can be generated can limit its practicality. This paper studies how to construct lightweight simulators for complicated systems. It focuses on environments where an agent directly interacts with only a small part of a larger system but still feels the effects of global dynamics.

The method pairs a local simulator with a learned model of the wider system’s influence. The local component handles the portion with which the agent interacts, while the learned component mimics effects arriving from outside that portion. This combination addresses the central difficulty of local simulation: the agent’s immediate surroundings do not evolve independently of the larger environment.

Experiments show that incorporating these influence-augmented local simulators into a deep reinforcement learning workflow can considerably accelerate training. The finding supports simulator design as a way to address the pace of experience generation. Its relevance is tied to the stated setting, where local interactions and wider influences can be treated through complementary simulation components.
icml-2022-influence-augmented-local-simu.tldr: Local simulators augmented with learned global influences can considerably accelerate reinforcement learning in the studied networked systems.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing provides a route to classifiers with certified robustness, but it also faces tradeoffs involving accuracy, certification, and fairness. Making the smoothing noise depend on the input has been proposed as a remedy. This paper examines whether such adaptations retain the formal basis needed for their robustness certificates.

The authors show that the input-dependent approaches they examine lack the required formal guarantees, leaving their certificates unjustified. More generally, they identify a curse of dimensionality that forces the variance function to have low semi-elasticity. This restricts how strongly the noise variance can respond to input changes and limits the flexibility that motivated input dependence.

The paper also supplies a theoretical and practical framework for using input-dependent smoothing under strict restrictions. A concrete variance-function design is tested on CIFAR10 and MNIST, where it mitigates some problems of classical smoothing while retaining formal support. The authors explicitly state that the design still needs improvement. The contribution therefore combines a warning about unsupported certification with a constrained route to justified adaptation.
icml-2022-intriguing-properties-of-input.tldr: Input-dependent smoothing faces dimensionality-driven restrictions, but a carefully constrained framework can support valid robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Distributed gradient computation must cope with slow workers and other faults. Coding schemes can help, but many approaches focus on recovering all worker data. This paper instead encodes partial derivatives directly and introduces lossy compression into the resulting derivative codewords, focusing on information useful for gradient-based learning.

The compression objective seeks to preserve information within codewords while reducing information shared between them. Its motivation comes from the observation that gradient descent can tolerate noise and that noise can sometimes help avoid overfitting and local minima. This supports allowing some information loss in the coded derivatives rather than treating exact recovery as the only useful outcome.

The scheme’s low-weight codes also allow iterative decoding, so a completed worker task can immediately contribute to the larger gradient update. That property enables asynchronous updates. Finally, the authors exploit the linear dependence of directional derivatives on direction vectors to apply linear coding techniques even within general machine learning frameworks such as deep neural networks. The contribution links compression, coding, and asynchronous optimization.
icml-2022-lightweight-projective-derivat.tldr: Coding and compressing derivatives directly enables iterative decoding and asynchronous gradient updates in distributed learning.

paragraphs: Model inversion attacks use a classifier’s learned knowledge to generate synthetic images reflecting characteristics of classes in its private training data. Earlier generative attacks rely on image priors tailored to a particular target model. That dependence makes them costly to prepare, less flexible, and vulnerable to differences between datasets.

Plug & Play Attacks reduce the dependence between the target classifier and the generative image prior. A single generative adversarial network can then support attacks against a range of targets with only minor adjustments. The authors also show that publicly available pretrained generators can support powerful attacks, extending the approach beyond generators specially prepared for a target.

The evaluation reports improved robustness and flexibility, including under strong distribution shifts where previous approaches fail to produce meaningful results. Generated images reveal sensitive class characteristics with high visual quality. The privacy finding concerns information about classes encoded in the model; the stated goal and evidence are synthetic class-representative images, rather than a claim of exact recovery of individual training images.
icml-2022-plug-play-attacks-towards-robu.tldr: Plug & Play Attacks reuse pretrained image generators across classifiers to reveal sensitive class characteristics, including under strong distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning applications require safety constraints to hold with probability one, also called almost surely. This is a demanding target for learning systems. Saute RL approaches it by reformulating the decision problem so that safety constraints become part of the state representation and the objective is reshaped.

The resulting Safety Augmented Markov Decision Process satisfies the Bellman equation. This matters because it connects the reformulated problem to a central structure used by reinforcement learning algorithms. The authors describe the approach as compatible with any RL algorithm through this augmentation, and they identify policy generalization across safety constraints as another capability enabled by the expanded state.

The paper presents the formulation as progress toward almost-sure constraint satisfaction, rather than claiming that every adapted learning algorithm automatically achieves it. Experiments show that Saute RL algorithms can outperform leading counterparts when satisfying constraints is especially important. The contribution is a reusable problem transformation that lets safety information shape decisions through the state and learning objective.
icml-2022-saute-rl-almost-surely-safe-re.tldr: Saute RL incorporates safety constraints into the state and objective, providing a reusable formulation aimed at almost-surely safe learning.

paragraphs: Orthogonal convolutions can help address vanishing or exploding gradients and sensitivity to perturbations. However, making a flattened convolution kernel orthogonal does not ensure that the convolution operation itself is orthogonal. This paper develops a framework that works at the level of the operation across diverse convolutional layers.

The authors establish an equivalence between orthogonal convolutions in the spatial domain and paraunitary systems in the spectral domain. Complete factorization of one-dimensional paraunitary systems lets them represent any separable orthogonal convolution as a composition of spatial filters. The resulting layers retain exact orthogonality while offering expressive power and improved memory and computational efficiency relative to previous designs.

The framework supports studying architectural choices including skip connections, initialization, stride, and dilation. The authors scale orthogonal networks to deep ResNet and ShuffleNet architectures, substantially outperforming shallower counterparts. They also construct residual flows, generative models requiring strict Lipschitz control. The work connects a mathematical characterization of convolution to practical designs for deeper orthogonal networks.
icml-2022-scaling-up-diverse-orthogonal-.tldr: A paraunitary framework enables expressive, exactly orthogonal convolutional layers and supports scaling them to deep network architectures.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions that earn rewards while consuming limited resources. Each available action has a context, and both its reward and resource consumption are linear functions of that context. The learner must maximize cumulative reward over a fixed horizon without exceeding the specified resource budgets.

The analysis uses a smoothed setting: Gaussian noise perturbs the base context vectors. The authors consider both stochastic base contexts and contexts chosen adversarially. In the stochastic case, they establish an O(√T) additive regret bound against the best fixed policy that can depend on context. Their approach combines greedy parameter estimation with a primal-dual treatment of resource constraints.

For adversarial base contexts, the main result is an algorithm with an O(log T) competitive ratio against the same type of policy comparator. It combines primal-dual ideas with a new adaptation of the doubling trick. This multiplicative comparison differs from the stochastic additive regret guarantee. Both results are established within the stated Gaussian-perturbation setting, which is central to the analysis.
icml-2022-smoothed-adversarial-linear-co.tldr: Under Gaussian-smoothed contexts, the paper provides resource-constrained bandit algorithms with stochastic regret and adversarial competitive-ratio guarantees.

paragraphs: Class imbalance is difficult in graph-based node classification because neighboring nodes interact during representation learning. Methods that compensate for minority classes using only their overall size overlook those connections. The paper identifies increased false positives among majority-class nodes as a consequence of treating minority nodes collectively in this way.

The authors hypothesize that the label distribution around each node strongly influences these false positives and confirm that relationship experimentally. Their proposed Topology-Aware Margin loss, or TAM, incorporates local graph structure into the training objective. It compares a node’s connectivity pattern with the average pattern for its class and adjusts the margin according to that comparison.

This gives the imbalance correction a node-specific component informed by connectivity, rather than relying solely on class counts. Across the reported node-classification benchmarks and representative graph neural network architectures, TAM consistently outperforms the baselines. The findings support accounting for where nodes sit in the graph when designing learning objectives for imbalanced classes, because local label structure affects the errors that class-level corrections can introduce.
icml-2022-tam-topology-aware-margin-loss.tldr: TAM adjusts classification margins using each node’s connectivity pattern to improve learning on class-imbalanced graphs.

paragraphs: Many network models group nodes into communities and assume that events between different node pairs are independent once those memberships are known. The paper identifies this assumption as an obstacle to reproducing higher-order patterns, such as triangles, that commonly appear in real networks. Its focus is on networks whose events occur in continuous time.

The proposed multivariate community Hawkes model, MULCH, introduces dependence between node pairs through structured multivariate Hawkes processes. It retains a community-based description while allowing relational events to be linked beyond what community membership alone captures. This expands the model’s ability to represent the interconnected patterns that motivate the work.

To fit MULCH, the authors combine spectral clustering with local refinement based on likelihood. They report much greater accuracy than existing models on both predictive and generative tasks. These two findings address complementary goals: predicting network events and generating network data. The results support explicitly modeling dependence between pairs as a useful extension of community-based continuous-time network models.
icml-2022-the-multivariate-community-haw.tldr: MULCH adds dependence between node pairs to community-based continuous-time network modeling, improving reported predictive and generative accuracy.
